The size at which females first achieve reproductive capability is relatively small; puberty is attained at a total length of 18.6 centimeters [Lp = 18.6 centimeters], a threshold that marks the onset of vitellogenesis and gonadal recrudescence. The early life stages of this species are characterized by rapid embryonic development within the constraints of a small egg. Based on an average egg diameter of 0.82 millimeters, the calculated wet weight at birth is approximately 0.00029 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00029 grams], placing the hatchling at the lower end of the mass spectrum for coral-reef teleosts. The rapid progression from chorion rupture to first prey capture is typical of pelagic-spawning carangiform fishes, minimizing the window of vulnerability to egg predators. Following this rapid hatch, the yolk-sac larva quickly transitions into a free-swimming, exogenously feeding planktonic larva, entering a period of intense growth and high mortality typical of the pelagic larval phase.

Females eventually attain a maximum wet weight of 579 grams [Wwi = 579 grams] at the conclusion of their growth period, a mass derived from length-weight relationships that describe the species as moderately elongate. This ultimate mass is achieved only after several years of sustained feeding on zooplankton in the mid-water column. At the point of puberty, however, when females are just 18.6 centimeters long, their corresponding body mass is substantially lower, with the wet weight at puberty calculated to be 65.3 grams [Wwp = 65.3 grams]. This considerable discrepancy between mass at maturity and ultimate mass underscores the energetic demands of continued somatic expansion while simultaneously supporting reproductive function through repeated spawning events over the course of many seasons.

This relatively short lifespan, in conjunction with small body size, positions the species as a fast-living member of the fish community on Indo-Pacific coral reefs.

While congeneric species such as Pterocaesio digramma may attain substantially larger adult sizes, the dark-banded fusilier reaches its terminal length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters] at a comparably earlier chronological age.
